summary: Robert James Fischer was an American chess grandmaster and the eleventh World Chess Champion. A prodigy, he won a record eight United States Championships, including the 1964 event with the only perfect score in its history. His rise was marked by independent preparation, exceptional competitive focus, and victories over leading Soviet and Western players.

Fischer qualified for the 1972 World Championship by defeating Mark Taimanov, Bent Larsen, and Tigran Petrosian, then defeated Boris Spassky in Reykjavík. The match became a major Cold War-era cultural event. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2785 in July 1972. Fischer later declined to defend the title under FIDE’s proposed conditions; in 1992 he won an unofficial rematch with Spassky.

summary: Vugar Gashimov was an Azerbaijani chess grandmaster, recognized especially for his strength in blitz chess. He became one of Azerbaijan’s leading players and reached a peak world ranking of sixth. His tournament career included victories and shared victories in strong international opens and invitation events.

Gashimov represented Azerbaijan at four Chess Olympiads and contributed to the country’s rise in team chess. He won the European Team Championship with Azerbaijan in Novi Sad in 2009, after the team had also taken bronze in 2007. His career was interrupted by serious illness, and he died in 2014 at the age of 27.

summary: Mikhail Tal was a Soviet Latvian chess grandmaster and the eighth World Chess Champion. He became renowned for imaginative attacking play, tactical complications, and a willingness to sacrifice material for initiative. His games and tournament performances made him one of the most influential and recognizable players in chess history.

Tal won the Soviet Championship several times and emerged through the Candidates cycle to challenge Mikhail Botvinnik. In 1960 he defeated Botvinnik to become the youngest world champion at that time. Health problems affected his later career, but he continued to compete at the highest level and remained a major force in Soviet chess.

summary: Viktor Korchnoi was a Soviet and later Swiss chess grandmaster and writer. He is widely regarded as one of the strongest players never to win the World Championship. His long career combined rigorous calculation, competitive resilience, and exceptional longevity across several generations of elite chess.

Korchnoi won the Soviet Championship four times and reached the World Championship match twice. He challenged Anatoly Karpov in 1978 and again in 1981, first as a Soviet defector and later as a Swiss representative. He remained a formidable tournament player well into old age, setting records for continued participation and high-level performance.

summary: Mikhail Botvinnik was a Soviet and Russian chess grandmaster, the sixth World Chess Champion, and one of the central figures of twentieth-century chess. He held the title in three separate reigns, combining systematic preparation with deep strategic understanding. His methods strongly influenced Soviet chess training and later generations of elite players.

Botvinnik won the Soviet Championship repeatedly and became world champion in 1948 after the postwar championship tournament. He regained the title from Vasily Smyslov in 1958 and from Mikhail Tal in 1961. Alongside chess, he worked as an electrical engineer and computer scientist and became an early pioneer of computer-chess research.

summary: Boris Vasilyevich Spassky was a Soviet and Russian chess grandmaster and the tenth World Chess Champion. Known for a broad, adaptable style, he was successful in both positional and tactical play. Spassky became one of the leading Soviet players during a period of exceptionally deep competition.

He played three World Championship matches. After losing to Tigran Petrosian in 1966, Spassky defeated Petrosian in 1969 to win the title. He lost the championship to Bobby Fischer in Reykjavík in 1972, in one of the most publicized matches in chess history. Spassky later remained active in international chess and played an unofficial rematch with Fischer in 1992.

He also appeared in international events including the Lublin Union Memorial. His life and playing career ended in 2013, leaving a comparatively brief record in the historical chess directory.

Timman won the Dutch Championship nine times and participated in the World Championship Candidates cycle on several occasions. He reached the 1993 FIDE World Championship match after the split in the world title structure, but lost to Anatoly Karpov. His career also included major tournament victories, extensive writing, and long service as a representative of Dutch chess.

He won the Soviet Championship twice and appeared in the World Championship Candidates cycle six times. Geller also won the Ukrainian SSR Championship four times. Late in his career, he shared first place in the 1991 World Seniors’ Championship and won the title outright in 1992, extending his competitive record across several decades.

Larsen was a frequent Candidates competitor and one of the most successful players in major international tournaments. He won the Interzonal tournaments in 1964 and 1967 and reached the Candidates final in 1968. He also led Denmark in Olympiad competition and helped establish a distinctive, ambitious style outside the Soviet chess tradition.

summary: Tigran Vardani Petrosian was a Soviet-Armenian chess grandmaster and the ninth World Chess Champion. Nicknamed Iron Tigran, he became famous for an almost impenetrable defensive style that emphasized safety, prophylaxis, and the prevention of counterplay. His success helped popularize chess in Armenia.

Petrosian won the World Championship in 1963 by defeating Mikhail Botvinnik and defended the title against Boris Spassky in 1966. He later lost the crown to Spassky in 1969. Petrosian was also a leading Soviet team player, winning multiple Chess Olympiad gold medals and contributing to the USSR’s dominant international record.

He played in seven Chess Olympiads, winning team gold with the Soviet Union at six. His opening research and writing, especially the Najdorf Sicilian variation that bears his name, became a lasting part of chess theory. His peak rating was 2645 in July 1972.

Hübner won or shared first in major events including Houston 1974, the 1979 Rio de Janeiro Interzonal, Chicago 1982, Biel 1984, and Linares and Tilburg in 1985. He served as Nigel Short’s second in the 1993 world championship match and won an Olympic team silver medal with Germany in 2000. His peak rating was 2640 in July 1981.

summary: David Bronstein was a Soviet and Russian grandmaster whose creative, tactical style made him one of the world’s strongest players from the mid-1940s into the 1970s. He tied for first in the 1948 and 1949 Soviet Championships, won the 1948 Saltsjöbaden Interzonal, and won the 1950 Candidates’ playoff against Isaac Boleslavsky to qualify for the world-title match.

Bronstein challenged Mikhail Botvinnik for the World Championship in 1951, drawing the match 12–12 after twenty-four games. He later competed in the 1953 Candidates’ Tournament and remained an influential analyst and writer. His Zurich International Chess Tournament 1953 is regarded as a classic chess book, preserving the ideas and character of one of the game’s great tournament eras.

Abramović represented Yugoslav chess at a high level and finished 16th–20th in the 1993 Biel Interzonal, an event in the World Championship qualification cycle. His later work included coaching and national-team selection, and FIDE awarded him the Senior Trainer title in 2013.

summary: Faruk Bistric was a Bosnian chess player who became International Master in 1997 and Grandmaster in 2003. He was recognized as a champion of Bosnia and Herzegovina and played for clubs including ŠK Bosna Sarajevo, Olimpik, Željezničar, and Bihać. He also worked for several years as a chess trainer in the United Arab Emirates.

Bistric represented Bosnia and Herzegovina at the 1998 and 2002 Chess Olympiads. He scored 3/5 on the team’s board in 1998 and 7.5/10 in 2002, when he earned his final Grandmaster norm in Bled. He later founded the BE AS ONE association and organized chess competitions.

summary: Petr Neuman was a Czech grandmaster who combined competitive chess with teaching mathematics and geography at a secondary school. In April 2013, he was one of 13 players tied for first at the Neckar Open and was ultimately placed tenth on tiebreak. He remained active in German league chess late in his career.

Neuman produced the strongest individual performance at the 2017 Czech Team Open Championship, scoring 6.5/7. In March 2025, shortly before his death, he finished second in the Pilsen Open E Blitz Rating Open with 9/11. He had just played for Bad Mergentheim in the German Bundesliga.

summary: Vasily Borisovich Malinin was a Soviet and Russian grandmaster who also held the ICCF correspondence Grandmaster title and the Russian Grandmaster title. His career combined over-the-board chess with an academic career in criminal law: he became a professor, earned a doctorate in law, and published more than 200 works, including monographs, textbooks, and legal encyclopedic material.

Malinin won the 21st Soviet Correspondence Championship in 2002 with 11.5/14, the final event spanning the transition from the USSR to Russia. He played first board for Saint Petersburg in the 10th Soviet Correspondence Team Championship, won an international tournament in Sukhumi in 2013, and won the Saint Petersburg veterans’ classical championship in 2017.

He finished fifth in the 1978 World Junior Championship and won the Argentine Championship in 1984. Barbero received the Grandmaster title in 1987 and became one of Argentina’s leading players during the 1980s and 1990s.

He represented Argentina in six Chess Olympiads between 1978 and 1994 and played on first board in 1990. Barbero moved to Budapest in 1986, where he continued his chess career and family life. His recorded victories included a notable win over Bent Larsen in Buenos Aires in 1991.

summary: Julio Bolbochán was an Argentine champion who won the national title in 1946 and 1948. He earned the International Master title in 1950 and became an International Grandmaster in 1977. His strongest tournament results included shared first place at Mar del Plata in 1951, 1952, and 1956, against fields featuring Erich Eliskases, Héctor Rossetto, and Miguel Najdorf.

Bolbochán represented Argentina in seven Chess Olympiads from 1950 through 1970. He qualified for the 1967 Sousse Interzonal but could not attend because the Argentine Chess Federation lacked funds for the trip. After 1976, he lived in Venezuela, where he taught chess and coached the Universidad Simón Bolívar Chess Club for more than 20 years.

Handoko earned the National Master title in 1978, progressed to FIDE Master and International Master in 1982, and became a Grandmaster in 1994.

Handoko represented Indonesia in the Chess Olympiad and the Asian Team Chess Championship. In 2003, he won the men’s masters tournament at the inaugural Japfa Chess Festival in Jakarta. His career peak came in the early 1990s, and he remained one of Indonesia’s most accomplished championship players.

summary: Abram Iosifovich Khasin was a Russian International Master and correspondence grandmaster, born in Zaporizhia in 1923. He served in the Red Army during World War II and lost both legs after being wounded at Stalingrad. After the war, he worked as an English teacher and chess coach, later living in Essen, Germany.

Khasin reached the finals of several USSR Championships and recorded major tournament results in Moscow, Hastings, Kislovodsk and Belgrade. He represented the USSR in the International Correspondence Chess Olympiads from 1968 to 1987, helping the team win three consecutive editions, and placed fourth in the 1975–1980 World Correspondence Championship.

Mirallès also made a substantial contribution as an administrator and educator. He served as technical director of the French Chess Federation from 1992 to 1996, collaborated with the magazine Échec et Mat, and later became president of the Geneva Chess Federation and director of the Geneva Chess School.

From 2005 to 2015, Henrichs helped SC Hansa Dortmund achieve two promotions to the 1. Bundesliga, sometimes playing on the top board. His recorded results included two grandmaster norms, victory at the Wil/SG Open with 4½/5, and a team-defining draw against David Navara.

Díez del Corral represented Spain at seven Chess Olympiads from 1960 to 1982, playing top board three times. At Varna in 1962 he won a bronze medal on second board with 10½/16. His tournament record also included second place at Amsterdam in 1969 and the 1975 Barcelona Zonal.

Early in his career he studied with Vladimir Bagirov and Vladimir Makogonov.

Guseinov won the Caucasus Championship in 1982, the Azerbaijan Championship in 1996, and several international tournaments. He represented Azerbaijan in team competitions for nearly three decades, including the 1998 Chess Olympiad and the 1997 European Team Championship, where he scored 6/9 on first board. He also coached the Qatar Chess Federation from 1991 to 1996.

summary: Karl-Heinz Podzielny jun. was a German International Master from Essen, recognized especially for his strength in blitz chess. He won the German Youth Championship in 1974, finished second at the 1974/75 European Youth Championship, and received the FIDE IM title in 1986. His best standard rating, reviewed by ChessEver, was 2512 in July 1999.

Podzielny won the German Blitz Championship seven times, in 1974, 1977, 1978, 1979, 1985, 1986, and 2007. He also won the German Rapid Championship in 2007, defended it in 2008 and 2009, and took the Goch Open in 2013. With Solinger SG 1868, he won the 1997 German Team Championship and reached the 1992 European Club Cup semifinal.

summary: Igor Yakovlevich Blechzin was a Soviet and Russian chess master, geographer, professor, and chess administrator. A leading young player in Leningrad during the late 1950s and early 1960s, he shared second place in the 1959 Soviet Youth Championship and won both the team and individual competitions with Leningrad at the 1960 Soviet republic-team championship. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2511 in October 2002.

Blechzin placed second in the 1962 Leningrad Championship and received the Soviet Master of Sport title in 1964 before becoming an International Master in 1995. He later served as vice-president of the Saint Petersburg Chess Federation. Outside chess, he earned a doctorate in geographical sciences in 1984, became a professor, and published research on environmental and economic geography as well as the 2003 book On Chess and More.

summary: Erich Gottlieb Eliskases was an Austrian-born grandmaster who represented Austria, Germany, Brazil, and Argentina. He became Tyrolean Champion at fifteen, shared the Austrian Championship at sixteen, and won the German Championship in 1938 and 1939. His strongest period came in 1938–39, when he won Noordwijk ahead of Paul Keres and Max Euwe and completed an eight-tournament unbeaten streak. ChessEver’s reviewed peak Classical rating was 2510 in June 1967.

Eliskases won or shared first at Budapest, Linz, Zürich, Milan, São Paulo, Mar del Plata, Punta del Este, and Córdoba. He represented three countries at Chess Olympiads and was granted the FIDE Grandmaster title in 1952. He served as Alexander Alekhine’s second in the 1937 rematch with Max Euwe and was renowned for endgame skill, including a celebrated victory over José Raúl Capablanca at Semmering in 1937.

summary: Alexander Alexandrovich Kotov was a Soviet grandmaster, Soviet champion, Candidates player, and influential chess author. He finished second in the 1939 USSR Championship, won the Soviet title jointly with David Bronstein in 1948, and won the 1950 Venice tournament ahead of Vasily Smyslov. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2510 in April 1968.

Kotov won the 1952 Saltsjöbaden Interzonal unbeaten with 16½/20, three points clear of Tigran Petrosian and Mark Taimanov, then competed in the 1953 Candidates Tournament. He represented the USSR at the 1952 and 1954 Olympiads, winning team gold medals. His books Think Like a Grandmaster, Play Like a Grandmaster, and Train Like a Grandmaster shaped generations of chess readers, while his analysis-tree method became known as the Kotov method.

summary: Edmar John Mednis was an American grandmaster and chess writer of Latvian origin. He finished second in the 1955 World Junior Championship behind Boris Spassky and became the first player to defeat Bobby Fischer in a United States Championship. Mednis also finished equal third in the 1961–62 U.S. Championship and played for the United States at the 1962 Chess Olympiad. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2510 in January 1979.

Mednis played in the 1979 Riga Interzonal, finished equal fourth at New York 1980, and shared first at Puerto Rico 1984. Awarded the FIDE Grandmaster title in 1980, he became especially influential as an author, writing 26 books and hundreds of articles. His works included How to Beat Bobby Fischer, Practical Rook Endings, and Strategic Chess: Mastering the Closed Game, with endgame technique a recurring focus.

summary: Igor Naumkin was a Russian grandmaster who earned the International Master title in 1988 and the Grandmaster title in 1990. He became known for an active tournament career across Europe after the collapse of the Soviet Union, eventually settling in Italy and becoming fluent in Italian. ChessEver’s reviewed peak Classical rating was 2510 in January 2007.

Naumkin recorded notable victories over former World Champion Mikhail Tal and grandmaster David Bronstein. His unusually busy schedule made him one of the most active grandmasters of 2019, when he played 258 games in 41 tournaments. Shortly before his death, he won a weekend tournament in Pegli with 4½/5. His career also included a 2017 six-month suspension following an attempted game-manipulation offer.

summary: András Ozsváth was a Hungarian FIDE Master, correspondence International Master, coach, organizer, journalist, and author. He became Budapest Champion in 1960, reached the Hungarian Championship finals in 1954, 1958, 1962, and 1965, and earned the FIDE Master title in 1980. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2510 in July 1971.

Ozsváth represented Budapest Honvéd for 27 years and served the club and its successors as coach and organizer for 38 years, winning eight team championships. He led Honvéd to second place in the 1988 European Club Cup final and represented Hungary several times between 1968 and 1982. As a correspondence player, he won Olympic team silver medals in 1977 and 1982. He also edited and wrote for Sakkélet and published several chess books.

summary: Hermann Pilnik was a German-born Argentine grandmaster who emigrated to Argentina in 1939. He won the Argentine Championship in 1942, 1945, and 1958, shared first at Mar del Plata in 1944, and won international tournaments including Beverwijk, Belgrade, and Stuttgart. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2510 in April 1968.

Pilnik represented Argentina in five Chess Olympiads. He won individual gold and team silver at Dubrovnik 1950, then added team silver medals at Helsinki 1952 and Amsterdam 1954, followed by team bronze at Munich 1958. He finished tenth in the 1956 Candidates Tournament, received the FIDE Grandmaster title in 1952, and later taught chess at the Caracas Military Academy. The Pilnik Variation of the Ruy Lopez bears his name.

He held the Grandmaster title and was part of a Hungarian generation that produced one of the country’s strongest Olympiad results. He reached the Czech Championship final tournaments, co-authored three chess books, and coached the Czech women’s team to seventh place at the 2009 European Team Championship in Novi Sad. He died on 11 July 2024.

summary: Lorenz Maximilian Drabke was a German International Master who represented Germany. His peak Classical rating was 2486 in July 2016.

Drabke served in the German Armed Forces and became a longstanding member of the NATO chess team. He won four individual NATO championships and eleven NATO team championships, while also playing Bundesliga chess for Schachgesellschaft Solingen and OSG Baden-Baden. He died in a traffic accident on 13 August 2018, aged 33.

summary: Volodia Vaisman was a Romanian-French chess player who became an International Master in 1975. Born in Bălți on 25 December 1937, he later studied at Alexandru Ioan Cuza University in Iași and worked as a Romanian teacher and chess player. His reviewed peak Classical rating was 2485 in January 1976.

In 1984, Vaisman left Romania with his wife during a tournament and settled in Montpellier, where he received political asylum and later French citizenship. He coached players including Sophie Milliet, helped Échecs Club Montpellier reach France's first division, and wrote several chess books. He died on 4 December 2023.

He won youth and memorial events, reached the semifinal of Hungary’s first knockout national championship, and earned a Grandmaster norm by winning the 2004 Elekes Grandmaster Tournament. He died on 12 October 2024.

He tied for first at the 2010 Pillsbury Memorial, shared the 2012 Ohio Chess Congress title, and placed third at the 2009 World Chess960 Championship. At the 1977 Asian Team Chess Championship he won team bronze and individual gold; he also earned team and individual bronze in 1979 and team silver in 1987 and 1989. He excelled at the Chess Olympiads, winning three individual gold medals, and was nominated as FIDE's official challenger to Alexander Alekhine in 1937. His legacy includes influential work on the Caro–Kann, Ruy Lopez, English, and Grünfeld openings.

summary: Héctor Decio Rossetto was an Argentine chess Grandmaster and a five-time Argentine Champion. He won the national title in 1942, 1944, 1947, 1962, and 1972, establishing a career that spanned Argentina’s postwar golden age of chess. He also won the Mar del Plata tournament in 1949 and 1952, sharing the latter victory with Julio Bolbochán.

Rossetto qualified for the 1964 Interzonal Tournament in Amsterdam and later served as director of the 1978 Chess Olympiad in Buenos Aires. FIDE awarded him the International Master title in 1950 and the Grandmaster title in 1960. He remained a central figure in Argentine chess across competition, organization, and national representation.

summary: Nicolas Rossolimo was a Russian-born, Greek-French-American chess Grandmaster and a celebrated cosmopolitan chess figure. He became a Paris champion a record seven times, won the French Championship in 1948, and finished second behind José Raúl Capablanca in a 1938 Paris tournament. He later emigrated to the United States and won the 1955 U.S. Open Championship.

Rossolimo represented France at the 1950 and 1972 Olympiads and the United States at the 1958, 1960, and 1966 Olympiads. FIDE awarded him the International Master title in 1950 and the Grandmaster title in 1953. The Rossolimo Variation of the Sicilian Defence bears his name, and he also ran a chess studio in New York while writing and recording music.

summary: Béla Perényi was a Hungarian chess International Master whose brief career became closely associated with opening theory. Born in 1953, he developed ideas in the Najdorf Sicilian that gave his name to two major variations, including the sharp Perényi Attack. His work was later used by leading grandmasters, among them Judit Polgár and Peter Leko.

Perényi reached a peak Classical rating of 2455 in July 1988. He died on 13 November 1988 in a car accident at age 35. His lasting contribution is theoretical rather than a long tournament record: the Perényi Attack remains identified with an enterprising piece sacrifice and concrete attacking play in the Najdorf Sicilian.

His tournament career included the 1955 World Junior Championship, the 1962 Stockholm Interzonal and repeated appearances in Argentine and South American championships. He reached a peak Classical rating of 2455 in January 1976 and died on 1 January 2017.

He later remained active in veteran competition, helping France win medals at the 2017 and 2019 World Senior Team Championships. His peak Classical rating was 2455 in January 1985; he died on 19 March 2024.

summary: Elena Tairova was a Belarusian and Russian chess player whose rapid rise brought two FIDE titles before she turned twenty. She won the European Youth Championship for girls under ten in 2001 while representing Belarus and the World Youth Championship for girls under fourteen in 2005 for Russia. She also won silver at the 2003 European under-twelve championship and bronze at the 2004 World Youth Championship.

The following year she helped Russia win silver at the first Women’s World Team Championship, tied for first in the Russian Superfinal and finished third in the Queens Woman Grandmasters tournament. She reached a peak Classical rating of 2455 in November 2009 and died on 16 March 2010 at age 18.

summary: Svein Johannessen was a Norwegian chess player who became the country's second International Master in 1961. He won the Norwegian Championship four times, taking the titles in 1959, 1962, 1970, and 1973. His broad opening repertoire included 1.d4, 1.e4, 1.c4, and 1.Nf3 with White, while his defenses with Black included the Open Games, Sicilian Defence, Old Indian Defence, and Queen's Gambit Accepted.

Johannessen represented Norway in ten Chess Olympiads from 1956 through 1978, scoring 86½ points in 152 games according to OlimpBase. His Olympiad record included an individual bronze medal at Lugano 1968 and strong individual performances at Varna 1962 and Skopje 1972. He was also the subject of a 2009 Norwegian chess biography by Øystein Brekke.

summary: Roman Shlemovich Pelts was a Ukrainian-Canadian chess player born in Odesa. He founded a chess school there in 1959, and seven of his early students later became grandmasters, including Lev Alburt, Sam Palatnik, Vladimir Tukmakov, Valeri Beim, Konstantin Lerner, Leonid Yurtaev, and Boris Kantsler. He was also the official trainer of the 1971 USSR student team.

Pelts played first board for the Soviet team that won the 1964 Students' World Championship in Kraków. After moving to Canada in 1978, he established the country’s first Canadian chess school in Montreal in 1979 and later continued in Toronto. He represented Canada at three Chess Olympiads, earned the FIDE Master title in 1981, and entered the Canadian Chess Hall of Fame in 2001.

summary: Jerzy Pokojowczyk was a Polish chess International Master and one of the country’s leading players from the late 1960s through the 1980s. He won silver medals in the Polish Junior Championships in 1968 and 1969, represented Poland at the 1969 European Junior Championship, and later participated twelve times in the Polish Chess Championship.

He developed into one of Croatia's strongest players during the 1960s and 1970s, combining tactical play with a long period of high-level competitive activity. He represented ŠK Slavonska banka, ŠK Slavonac of Našice and ŠK Polet of Buševec.

Košanski won the individual Croatian championship in 1972 and maintained a rating above 2400 for 25 years, according to his Croatian biography. His recorded results also include victory in the 1989 Budapest tournament and fifth place in the first Open Championship of independent Croatia. He died in Bjelovar on 21 November 2009, aged 68, after a career that made him a notable figure in Croatian chess.

summary: Ladislav Mišta was a Czech chess player who represented Czechoslovakia until 1990. He earned the International Master title in 1971 and built a substantial tournament career across Central Europe. His early results included shared second place in the 1959 Czechoslovak under-16 championship and third place in the 1966 Czechoslovak army championship.

Mišta represented Czechoslovakia at the 1968 World Student Team Championship in Ybbs and won the 11th Reggio Emilia New Year's tournament in 1968–69 on tiebreak ahead of Victor Ciocaltea, Ivan Radulov and Enrico Paoli. He also won international tournaments in Olomouc in 1967, 1970 and 1979 and in Zamárdi in 1980, sharing first place at Moscow in 1973 and Ostrava in 1980. He died in June 2010.

summary: Risto Nicevski was a Yugoslav and later North Macedonian chess player from Bitola who received the International Master title in 1975. His career included appearances in Yugoslav championships, international events, a zonal tournament and team competitions, placing him among the leading players from the region during the 1960s and 1970s.

Nicevski scored 8½/17 and shared ninth to tenth place in the 1969 Athens zonal tournament. He scored 1/2 for Yugoslavia at the 1970 European Team Championship in Kapfenberg, won an international tournament in Kragujevac in 1980 with 9/13, and competed in several Rubinstein Memorial editions at Polanica-Zdrój. He died in Yerevan on 18 September 1996, aged 51.

Nikolić won international tournaments in San Benedetto, Bari, La Spezia, Beverwijk, Biel, Ravenna, Smederevska Palanka and Brighton. He was also Macedonian champion in Probištip in 1963 and represented Yugoslavia against the Soviet Union and Hungary in 1967. Nun's strongest results came in correspondence chess: he won two Czechoslovak championships and represented Czechoslovakia in correspondence Olympiads. The Czechoslovak team won the fifth Olympiad in 1968 and finished second in 1972; his game against Estrin became notable for its opening. summary: Alla Shulimovna Kushnir, later Kushnir-Stein, was a Soviet-born Israeli chess player and a professor of classics, numismatics, and archaeology. She received the Woman International Master title in 1962, became a Woman Grandmaster in 1976, reached a peak Classical rating of 2430 in January 1990, and entered the World Chess Hall of Fame in 2017.

Kushnir challenged Nona Gaprindashvili three times for the Women's World Championship, in 1965, 1969, and 1972. She won three Women's Chess Olympiads: with the Soviet team in 1969 and 1972, and with Israel in 1976. Her tournament victories included Subotica, Belgrade, Moscow, Vrnjačka Banja, and the 1976 Roosendaal Interzonal.

summary: Béla Lengyel was a Hungarian chess player and International Master. He became a first-category player in 1967, a candidate master in 1968, and a Hungarian master in 1970. In 1975 he won the Hungarian championship semifinal and achieved his first International Master norm. He later became a two-time Budapest champion in 1979 and 1980, earning the International Master title in 1985.

Lengyel remained active in strong tournament chess for decades, including regular appearances in the First Saturday events from 1992. He won the April 2002 First Saturday tournament and finished joint second or third at the inaugural Zsámbék Open in 2006. His recorded peak Classical rating at 2430 in January 1987.

Malbrán represented Argentina at the 1998 Chess Olympiad in Elista. The Argentine Chess Federation announced his death in 2025 and described him as a distinguished figure in Argentine chess. Trois represented Brazil at the Chess Olympiads of 1972, 1978, and 1982. He received the International Arbiter title in 1986 and remained a significant figure in Brazilian tournament chess. The recorded peak Classical rating as 2430 in July 1984. He died on 16 September 2020.

Zsinka served as a member of the Budapest General Assembly from 1998 to 2006 and led the MIÉP parliamentary group from 2001. summary: Salvador Díaz Carias (23 June 1933 - 2022) was a Venezuelan FIDE Master whose Classical rating peaked at 2121 in July 2012. One of Venezuela’s leading players from the 1950s onward, he won the national championship in 1960 and again in 1978.
